title: Sorrow That Leads to Change
overview: Paul tells the church in Corinth how relieved and glad he is that his painful letter led them to set things right and renew their friendship with him.

parts.label: A call to clean living (v. 1)
parts.note: "These promises" points back to the end of chapter 6, where God promises to live among his people and be their Father. Because of that, Paul urges them to turn away from anything that spoils body or spirit, out of deep respect for God.

parts.label: Make room for us (vv. 2-4)
parts.note: Paul asks them to open their hearts to him, insisting he has not cheated, misled or taken advantage of anyone, likely answering charges spread by rival teachers. He says this not to blame them but because he loves them so much he would live or die with them.

parts.label: Comfort when Titus came (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: This picks up the story from chapter 2, where Paul was anxiously waiting for news from his coworker Titus, who had gone to Corinth. In Macedonia (northern Greece) he faced trouble outside and fear inside, until Titus arrived saying the Corinthians missed Paul and were sorry.

parts.label: A painful letter (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: Paul had written a sharp letter that hurt them; it may be 1 Corinthians, but many scholars think it was a now lost "tearful letter" mentioned in 2:4. He had second thoughts, but is glad now because their grief led them to change course, unlike sorrow that only regrets the consequences and ends in ruin.

parts.label: Signs of real change (vv. 11-13a)
parts.note: Their sorrow showed in eagerness to clear themselves, anger at the wrong done, and readiness to see it dealt with. Who did the wrong is unclear: older readers link it to the man in 1 Corinthians 5 who took his father's wife, while many modern scholars think someone in the church had openly attacked Paul.

parts.label: Titus's joy (vv. 13b-16)
parts.note: Paul had praised the Corinthians to Titus before sending him, and their warm welcome proved him right. They received Titus "with fear and trembling," a phrase most readers take to mean humble seriousness and respect rather than actual terror.

think: Can you remember a time when someone told you a hard truth that hurt at first, and what made the difference between it helping you and simply wounding you?
